Life 10 October 2026

Two languages, one desk

I write in French at night and in English by day, from a house in Maryland, for readers in Douala and in Baltimore. It is not a conflict. It is the desk.

By day I run networks: cloud and infrastructure for a large organisation, the kind of work where a quiet afternoon is the goal. By night I build the rest, and the language changes with the project. Uplink and Lemon speak English because their readers do. Bobine, Droit Facile and the books speak French first because the people I wrote them for think in French, and because French is where my sentences come out with their rhythm intact.

I grew up with the palaver, the idea that a decision is argued in public until it holds. It shows up everywhere in what I make. Droit Facile explains the law in plain words because the law belongs to the people it governs. The essays are written to be read aloud in a classroom or a neighbourhood meeting. Even the project book is a kind of palaver: everything on the table, everything priced, sign when you agree.

People ask which one I am, the network engineer or the writer. I am the desk. Both happen there, often the same evening, and the one feeds the other: the engineer gives the writer structure, the writer gives the engineer a sentence an owner can understand.

If you are bilingual and building something, let it be bilingual from the first screen. The toggle at the top of this page took an hour. Not having it would have cost me half my readers.
